Subject: Surcharge shelf-life on Exhibit B — need a quick clarification

Hi Tessa,

We're reviewing the draft Exhibit B (attached) and there is one operational point our procurement team wants clarified before we accept the schedule: the term 'shelf-life' used in section 3.2 (surcharges & reactivation). The language currently reads a bit high level and our billing team needs a deterministic rule for invoicing/credits. Two specific asks from our side: 

- Does 'shelf-life' mean the surcharge remains available to the customer for a defined period after the committed window (e.g., 12 months from invoice) even if not used? Or is it a rolling window tied to invoice dates?
- If a credit or true-up is issued, does the credit reduce the surcharge bucket first or the base commitment? In other words, how do credits interact with the surplus surcharge credits in the same accounting period?

Example: if Nimbus has a 6-month commit and we apply a temporary surcharge in month 2, what happens to that surcharge if the customer reduces usage in month 4 — do we carry it forward, expire it, or offset it against future invoices?

We attached ExhibitB_v5.pdf with a couple of inline comments (PDF annotations). If you can confirm the intended behavior and, if helpful, propose a short redline that defines 'shelf-life' with an example, that would help us close the loop with finance.

Thanks — appreciate a quick turnaround on this if possible.

Best,
Laura Gomez
Senior Procurement Manager
Nimbus Health
[Attachment: ExhibitB_v5.pdf (pdf)]

Subject: Re: Surcharge shelf-life on Exhibit B — need a quick clarification

Hi Laura — thanks for the clear examples, that helps.

Short answer: the intent behind the 'shelf-life' language was to give customers a predictable period to consume surcharge credits following a charge event, not to create an open-ended balance. Practically speaking we intended a 12-month consumption window tied to the invoice date that generated the surcharge (so "12 months from invoice"), with any unused surcharge credit expiring at the end of that window.

That said, Ben and I discussed internally and we agree that the contract should state this explicitly and include a worked example (your example is great). Proposed redline (draft snippet attached):

"Shelf-life" means the period beginning on the invoice date that first records a surcharge event and ending 12 months thereafter. During the Shelf-life period, surcharge credits may be applied against subsequent invoices for the same account. Any unused surcharge credits will expire at the end of the applicable Shelf-life period and will not carry forward thereafter.

I'll also attach a short note with the example for inclusion in the exhibit. If Procurement Legal is comfortable, this should be a small, non-substantive clarification that closes the operational gap.

Attached: ExhibitB_ShelfLife_Notes.docx (proposed snippet + example).

Next steps: Ben, Karthik — can you confirm this wording is acceptable operationally and whether we need any linkage to the commitment true-up mechanics (e.g., ordering of credits vs. base true-up)? If not, we'll propose the redline to Nimbus as-is.

Thanks,
Tessa Morgan
Sr. Manager, Commercial Contracts
Redwood Inference
[Attachment: ExhibitB_ShelfLife_Notes.docx (docx)]

Tessa — quick operational note from billing: the 12-month-from-invoice approach is workable, but two clarifications we should bake into the snippet to avoid disputes later: 

1) Ordering rule for adjustments: specify that invoice-level credits (e.g., billing corrections) are applied before surcharge consumption (or vice-versa) — we recommend credits apply first to reduce outstanding base charges, then to surcharge buckets. That prevents customers from manufacturing a credit to preserve a surcharge credit.

2) Interaction with true-up: when a commitment true-up occurs (annual/prorated), treat surcharge credits as distinct from committed usage reconciliation; surcharge credits cannot reduce committed usage obligations. That prevents the customer from using surcharge credits to eat into committed minimums.

Suggested short additions (to your snippet):

- "Ordering of adjustments: Any invoice credit or billing correction shall be applied first to outstanding base charges, then to any available surcharge credits."

- "True-up interaction: Surcharge credits are accounted for separately and may not be applied to reduce committed usage or cash obligations resulting from the commitment true-up process."

If we include those two lines the billing team can implement without special-case logic.

Ben
Director, Revenue Operations
Redwood Inference

That helps our accounting team reconcile balances.

We are otherwise comfortable with the 12-month window and the separate-true-up language, but the FIFO note on billing corrections would be useful. I've attached our procurement questionnaire for completeness.

If that's acceptable, we can sign off on the exhibit and ask our legal team to accept the small change.
